title: bench harness stepped warmup noise protocol
content:
Purpose
This note captures a pragmatic, experiment-focused methodology for running throughput benchmarks that emphasize repeatability while explicitly measuring and mitigating noise sources. The objective: consistent throughput curves and defensible p95/p99 latency numbers across repeated runs, plus a set of profiling checks that quickly surface bottlenecks.

Scope
- Applies to GPU-backed model serving experiments in the Redwood runtime (inference-only workloads).
- Focus on token-generation throughput and latency under steady and ramping loads.
- Includes guidance for single-model and mixed-model workloads, short/long sequences, and KV cache hotness variations.

High-level goals
- Produce a clear steady-state throughput number with confidence intervals.
- Avoid optimistic numbers that occur only during transient warmup or one-off favorable scheduling.
- Surface common sources of variance (thermal, kernel-selection thrash, batching variability, preemption).

Key definitions used in experiments
- Warmup phase: initial period where caches, kernels, and runtimes prime; measurements ignored.
- Stepped warmup: a sequence of discrete QPS/clients/seq_len steps that stabilizes batching and cache behavior before target load.
- Steady-state window: contiguous time window after warmup used for metric aggregation.
- Hot fraction: fraction of requests that hit a primed KV/prefix cache.

Testbed and baseline setup (minimum)
- Host: r5d.8x or equivalent for CPU-bound preprocess; GPU: A10G / A100 (specify exact driver and CUDA).
- Runtime: commit hash + build-id; Docker image tag recorded for each run.
- System settings locked: governor=performance; SMT disabled if historically noisy; cgroup limits pinned for memory and CPU.
- Network isolation: loopback loadgen preferred; if traffic must cross NIC, pin IRQs and use dedicated pNIC.
- Power/thermal: ensure node has been idle for 15+ minutes or run 10m soak before experiments.

Load generator configuration patterns
1) Stepped warmup (recommended default)
   - Sequence: 0 -> 20% -> 40% -> 60% -> 80% -> target QPS (each step 60–90s).
   - At each step: fixed client count, fixed request distribution, ensure no autoscaling changes.
   - Rationale: lets batching and kernel selection settle gradually; reveals non-linear transitions.
2) Linear ramp (alternative)
   - Smooth increase from 0 to target over 5–10 minutes; useful for assessing graceful degradation.
3) Burst / sawtooth (stress test)
   - Short bursts above target to check fallback policies, cold-kernel cache misses.
4) Trace-replay (for reproducibility)
   - Exact sequence of requests saved and replayed with same timing and seeds. Use for regression comparisons.

Warmup best practices
- Use stepped warmup by default. Each step must be long enough for KV cache to stabilize and a few batch-size cycles to occur (typically 1–2 minutes at each step).
- Warmup must match production-like request characteristics: same prompt length distribution and hot-prefix ratio.
- Save a warmup snapshot (experiment metadata) describing step durations, observed batch histograms, and kernel choices.

Repeatability and noise control
- Determinism: pin random seeds in loadgen client and model-serving layers where supported.
- Fixed ephemeral ids: disable ephemeral session creation that injects jitter into routing decisions.
- Environment snapshot: capture kernel version, nvidia-smi output, driver/CUDA versions, PCI bus topology, NUMA map.
- Run N independent trials (N >= 3) and report mean and standard deviation; prefer reporting median and IQR for skewed latency distributions.

Measurement windows and metrics to record
- Primary metrics (collected at 1s granularity): total_tokens/s, requests/s, p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (server-side per request), batch_size histogram, queue_length, GPU_util, GPU_mem_util, SM_occupancy (if available).
- Secondary metrics: CPU % per core, interrupts/sec, context_switches, disk IO (if swapping), network retransmits, temperature, power draw.
- Profiling traces: high-granularity timeline for a short slice (see profiling hooks).
- Save raw loadgen logs, runtime internal traces, and GPU traces with timestamps aligned to a common clock.

Signal processing and analysis
- Ignore the initial warmup window entirely.
- Use rolling-window percentile (30s window) to find stable periods; choose a contiguous steady-state window of at least 2m where rolling p95 variance < 5%.
- Remove obvious outliers caused by infra events (document and keep raw logs).
- Report both instantaneous peak throughput (best 1m window) and sustainable throughput (median over steady-state window).

Profiling hooks and quick checks
- Lightweight checks (run before full profiling): nvidia-smi sampling (1s), top/htop, iostat, sar. Look for CPU steal, runaway IO, or thermal throttling.
- GPU traces: use Nsight Systems for end-to-end timelines, and CUPTI-based sampling for kernel-level durations. Capture 30–60s around steady-state.
- PyTorch/C++ runtime traces: instrument token-level events (request-recv, preprocess, forward-start, forward-end, postprocess, send). Correlate with GPU kernel times.
- Kernel-selection noise: capture which kernel variants are chosen over time; if switching observed, try forcing a kernel or adjust sequence-length heuristics to stabilize.

Common failure modes and diagnostics
- High variance despite long warmup: check for non-deterministic kernel selection or thermal cycling. Re-run with smaller step increments and longer hold times.
- Sudden throughput drops mid-run: examine host dmesg for OOM or GPU reset; check cgroup reclaiming.
- Batch size oscillation: inspect request arrival patterns; add jitter in loadgen to avoid pathological alignment unless you want to test that case.
- Cross-tenant interference (Dedicated): verify isolation via CPU pinning and PCI bus checks; run a baseline idle probe.

Experiment naming and artifact capture
- Naming convention: bench.<model>.<seqlen>.<workload>.<target-qps>.<date> e.g. bench.gpt-small.512.steady.120qps.2025-01-14
- For each run save: loadgen-config.jsonl, runtime-trace.jsonl, nvidia-smi.log, nsight-sys.qdrep (if used), environment.txt. Bundle into an artifacts tarball and upload to the bench storage bucket.

Example experiment plan (template)
- model: llama-7b-v1
- sequence_lengths: 64, 256, 1024 (separate runs)
- warmup: stepped 6 steps (0,20,40,60,80,target) hold 75s each
- target: 200 requests/s
- trials: 5 independent trials per seq_len
- profiling: Nsight captures for trial 3 only
- record: all raw logs and a short human-readable summary of anomalies

Quick reproducibility checklist (pre-run)
- [ ] Confirm image tag and runtime commit hash written to experiment metadata
- [ ] Pin CPU and GPU governors, disable turbo if noisy
- [ ] Ensure no unrelated batch jobs on node; run 10m idle soak or restart node
- [ ] Capture baseline nvidia-smi, dmesg, and uname -a
- [ ] Start loadgen with deterministic seed and ensure trace saving enabled

Post-run analysis quick steps
- Aggregate run-level metrics and compute median/IQR across trials
- Compare batch histograms between trials to spot systematic differences
- Inspect GPU kernel timeline for unexpected kernels or long memcpy periods
- If noise > 10% CV in throughput: re-run with extended warmup or disable suspected noisy subsystem

Notes / open questions
- How much warmup time is model dependent? Empirically some models settle in two steps; others need many more due to kernel jit/caching. We should build a small automated routine that probes stability and recommends step hold times.
- Investigate whether a short synthetic micro-workload can deterministically prime kernels and caches without needing the full warmup sequence.

Appendix: quick commands
- capture env: echo $(date) > environment.txt; uname -a >> environment.txt; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version,temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 > nvidia-smi.log &
- basic nsight start: nsight-sys --capture=mycap.qdrep --target-pid=<runtime-pid> --duration=60
- perf sample: perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30; perf script > perf.unfolded

If this approach looks useful we can convert warmup heuristics into a small library in the loadgen so experiments can auto-propose step durations and detect instability automatically.

Authors: Ava Martinez (primary), notes and templates contributed by Julian Park and Maya Singh.

End of document.
